Colorado statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord must return the security deposit or mail a written statement of exact reasons within 30 days after the lease ends or the premises are surrendered; a written lease may extend this up to 60 days (C.R.S. 38-12-103(1)). (Security Deposits, Judicial Legal Help Center (cites C.R.S. 38-12-103); source)
  • A landlord who wrongfully keeps a deposit may be liable for triple damages plus attorney fees and costs; tenant must give written notice of intent to sue at least 7 days before filing. (Security Deposits, Judicial Legal Help Center (C.R.S. 38-12-103); source)
  • HB25-1249 (effective Jan 1, 2026) requires a walk-through inspection on request, bars retaining deposit for preexisting damage, presumes bad faith if amount retained is 125% or more of actual damages, and requires transfer or return of a deposit within 60 days after the landlord's interest in the unit ends. (HB25-1249 Tenant Security Deposit Protections; source)
  • Warranty of habitability defense, C.R.S. 38-12-503: tenant must give written notice of the condition stating the landlord has five days to repair (unless tenant caused it). (Residential Evictions, Colorado Judicial Branch; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Colorado law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Demand for Compliance (JDF 99 A) is used for late rent or lease violation; time to comply is between 3 and 30 days depending on the rental agreement; must be in tenant's primary language. (Residential Evictions, Colorado Judicial Branch; source)
  • Notice to Terminate Tenancy (JDF 99 B) is for repeated or substantial lease violation or criminal behavior; notice period 1 to 91 days depending on the rental agreement. (Residential Evictions, Colorado Judicial Branch; source)
  • Notice of No-Fault Eviction (JDF 99 C), for demolition/conversion, substantial repairs, landlord use, sale of the home, or no new rental agreement, requires at least 90 days; C.R.S. 38-12-1303 requires cause for eviction. (Residential Evictions, Colorado Judicial Branch; C.R.S. 38-12-1303; source)
  • Eviction (FED) is filed in the county where the property is located; after a judgment, a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) lets the Sheriff physically remove the tenant; court usually gives tenant 48 hours to leave. (Residential Evictions, Colorado Judicial Branch; source)
